WPGM Reviews: Tramlines Festival 2026

Live Reviews, Reviews
Share the article:
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 4:34
Instaread

There are few better feelings as a music fan than watching an artist you grew up with from the other side of the barrier. Suddenly the songs that once soundtracked your childhood are now being captured through your own lens. Tramlines 2026 gave me that feeling more than once.

Three days in Hillsborough Park brought together some of the biggest names in British music alongside artists who are still finding their feet, and while the headline performances delivered everything you’d expect from a festival of this size, it was the moments of personal nostalgia that stayed with me most.

Friday started with The Vaccines, a band I’ve now seen three times but, until this weekend, never had the opportunity to photograph, which was a surreal feeling as a band that has been a staple of my childhood and many others’ continued to perform their biggest hits on a festival stage.

The crowd clearly felt the same connection, with The Vaccines going down well before Kaiser Chiefs brought another collection of familiar anthems to Hillsborough Park. Fatboy Slim would eventually headline Friday, proving as popular as expected, while The K’s, Black Honey, The Clause and Radio Free Alice gave plenty of reason to explore beyond the main stage.

Saturday brought another couple of those surreal moments. As an indie lover, there are certain songs that feel bigger than the bands that wrote them. Blossoms’ “Your Girlfriend” and Courteeners’ “Not Nineteen Forever” are two of those songs for me. They are part of the soundtrack to growing up with British indie music, so being able to photograph both artists at Tramlines was something I don’t think I’ll ever take for granted.

There is something strange about hearing thousands of people sing back a song that you’ve known for years while you’re standing in the photographers’ pit trying to capture the moment.

Blossoms delivered exactly the kind of festival performance you’d hope for, while Courteeners took on the headline slot and gave their audience the anthems they had come for. For the crowd, it was a chance to relive songs that have become part of their own lives. For me, it was another opportunity to photograph music that has been part of mine.

Saturday wasn’t only about nostalgia, though. Rick Astley and Gabrielle brought their own generations of fans together, while Freddie Halkon, Seb Lowe, Girl In The Year Above, Sleeper and Everly Pregnant Brothers added to an already packed day.

Then Sunday saw the festival begin its final push, with Wolf Alice, Wet Leg, The Enemy, Reverend & The Makers, Lottery Winners and Florence Road among those keeping Hillsborough Park moving.

The Royston Club was another personal highlight. They just keep getting better and better. Whether it’s the music itself or what they are like live, there’s a confidence developing around The Royston Club that makes it very easy to understand why they are so loved. Every time I see them, they seem to have taken another step forward, and Tramlines was no different.

Then came the performance that would become my highlight of the entire weekend. Bleech 9:3. Playing to a packed Leadmill Stage, they completely blew the roof off. The best festival discoveries you don’t see coming. There were people in that room who didn’t know Bleech 9:3 when they walked in, but by the time they left, they certainly understood them.

There are elements of Wunderhorse in their sound and, if this performance was anything to go by, I wouldn’t be surprised to see Bleech 9:3 follow a similar trajectory in terms of notoriety. The energy was undeniable. The room was packed. Their performance demanded attention. That’s what festivals like Tramlines are supposed to do. And they do it well.

Of course, Wolf Alice had the honour of closing the weekend, bringing three days of music to an end from the main stage. But while the headline performances gave us the huge crowds and familiar songs, it was the smaller moments that made this Tramlines particularly memorable.

Photographing The Vaccines after growing up with their music. Standing in front of Blossoms and Courteeners while thousands sang songs that have been part of my own indie soundtrack. Watching The Royston Club continue to grow. And discovering Bleech 9:3 at exactly the kind of stage where a future festival favourite can begin to emerge.

Tramlines 2026 was full of those moments. Some took me back. And some made me wonder who we might all be talking about next.

Words + photography by Aaron Bruce
